description: Spring Boot starter for Telegram-bot based registration and authentication. A client opens a login session, the user confirms in a Telegram bot, and the backend returns a host-defined payload such as a JWT. Supports several user types, each with its own bot, tables and REST prefix, plus optional contact sharing, number matching, managed bots and white-label tenant bots.
rules: Set telegram.auth.enabled: true; the auto-configuration stays off when it is missing or false.

The starter creates no tables, entities, controllers or bots. For each user type, subclass BaseTelegramUser, BaseAuthSession, BaseTelegramUserRepository, BaseAuthSessionRepository, AbstractTelegramUserService, AbstractSessionService and AbstractTelegramAuthController, and provide TelegramBotModule and DefaultAuthFlow beans in one @Configuration.
Table names come from @Table on your entity subclasses and the REST prefix comes from @RequestMapping on your controller subclass, not from configuration properties.
Give every user type its own TelegramBotModule and pass it explicitly to that type's session service, controller and flow.
Index ip_address on each auth-session table, because every POST /session counts pending sessions per IP.
When upgrading from 0.4.x to 0.5.0, add the nullable host_ref VARCHAR(128) column to every auth-session table.

Mini App login is opt-in: call .miniApp(MiniAppOptions.defaults()) on the TelegramBotModule builder and use the 3-arg AbstractTelegramAuthController constructor (sessionService, module, userService), and map the route in your subclass: @PostMapping("/miniapp") public ResponseEntity<?> miniApp(@RequestBody(required = false) Map<String, Object> body, HttpServletRequest req) { return miniAppLogin(body, req); }. The base class maps nothing, so upgrading adds no route. The endpoint takes {"initData": "..."}.
Run a single application instance: the transport is long polling and the event bus is in memory.
